summary: Describes a method for compressing the IP, UDP and RTP headers of audio and video packets to cut overhead on low-speed serial links. Because these headers are large compared with small voice packets, compressing them makes better use of limited bandwidth.

eli5.summary: Voice packets are tiny but wear huge labels. This document shows how to shrink the labels so phone calls fit better over slow wires.

questions: how small does crtp make ip udp rtp headers
what is a compression context id
subtitle: How to squeeze the 40 bytes of IP, UDP and RTP headers down to 2-4 bytes on slow dial-up links.

tldr.problem: The 12-byte RTP header is a large overhead for 20-byte audio payloads on low-speed lines such as dial-up modems at 14.4 or 28.8 kb/s.
tldr.mechanism: The two ends of a link keep shared state for each stream and send only what changed in a compact form, so the combined IP, UDP and RTP headers usually shrink to 2 bytes, or 4 with UDP checksums.
tldr.outcome: In many cases all three headers compress to 2-4 bytes. RFC 2508 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 2508 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is designed to fit within the header compression framework of RFC 2507.

sections.title: The Header Overhead Problem
sections.content:
RTP is the Real-time Transport Protocol used for network audio and video. Its 12-byte header is a heavy overhead for 20-byte payloads when the line is a dial-up modem running at 14.4 or 28.8 kb/s. Some applications in this setting used an application-specific protocol with a header of a few bytes, but with less functionality than RTP.

The authors compare two options: compress the RTP header alone, end to end, or compress the combined IP, UDP and RTP headers, link by link. Compressing the 40 bytes of combined headers gives substantially more gain than compressing 12 bytes of RTP alone, because the result is about the same size (2-4 bytes) either way. Link-by-link compression also performs better because delay and loss are lower. So this RFC defines combined compression of IP, UDP and RTP headers on a link-by-link basis.

The scheme works with IPv4, IPv6 or packets with more than one IP header, though the initial focus is IPv4. It fits into the general compression framework of RFC 2507 as a third class of packet, carved out of the non-TCP class, and it builds on the design of TCP/IP header compression in RFC 1144.
sections.eli5: A tiny voice packet carries a big label with the sender, receiver and other details. On a slow phone line, the label takes more room than the message. This document shrinks the label.

sections.title: Assumptions and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The goal is to cut the IP/UDP/RTP headers to two bytes for most packets when no UDP checksums are sent, or four bytes with checksums. The target is audio and video over 14.4 and 28.8 dial-up modems. Those links tend to be full duplex, and the protocol uses that: the receiving end can send an explicit error signal back, which shortens recovery compared with periodically refreshing with an uncompressed header. The scheme performs best on local links with low round-trip time and can be used with reduced performance on simplex links.

The RFC keeps the scheme narrow on purpose. It does not define segmentation or preemption of large packets, which is left to a separate layer. The compression needs only that the link layer provides some packet type codes, a packet length indication and good error detection. Implementation simplicity matters too: a communications server may need to support compression over perhaps as many as 100 dial-up modem lines using a single processor.

The RFC also argues for compressing IP/UDP and RTP together. Compressing them separately loses too much of the gain, and crossing the layer boundary is appropriate because the same function is applied across all of them.
sections.eli5: The designers picked a simple fix for slow phone lines where talking goes both ways. If something goes wrong, one end can quickly tell the other, instead of waiting for a full reset.

sections.title: The Basic Idea: Shared Context
sections.content:
In TCP header compression, about half of the header bytes stay constant for the life of a connection, so they are sent once and then left out. RTP compression adds a bigger trick. Several fields change in every packet, but the change from one packet to the next is often constant, so the second-order difference is zero. The compressor and decompressor both keep the last full header and the first-order differences. Then all that must be sent is an indication that the second-order difference was zero, and the decompressor rebuilds the header by adding the stored differences to the saved one, with no loss of information.

State is kept per stream in a session context, defined by the IP source and destination addresses, the UDP source and destination ports, and the RTP SSRC field. Each compressed packet carries a small integer, the context identifier (CID), so the decompressor can look up the right context directly.

Because the compression is lossless, it can be applied to any UDP traffic that benefits. A compressor may guess whether a packet is RTP, since no harm is done if the guess is wrong. It will usually keep a negative cache of streams that failed to compress as RTP, for example because the SSRC keeps changing, so they do not use up all the contexts. When RTP compression fails, the IP and UDP headers may still be compressed.
sections.eli5: If a counter goes up by the same amount every time, you only need to say 'same step again'. Both sides remember the last number and the step size, so they can work out the next one without being told.

sections.title: Packet Types and the Compressed Header
sections.content:
The link layer must be able to tell apart four new packet formats, in addition to normal IPv4 and IPv6 packets:

  • FULL_HEADER: the uncompressed headers, sent to set up the context. It also carries the context ID and a 4-bit sequence number, tucked into the length fields of the IP and UDP headers, since the real length can be taken from the link layer.
  • COMPRESSED_UDP: IP and UDP headers compressed to 6 or fewer bytes (often 2 if UDP checksums are off), followed by the rest uncompressed. It is used when the usually constant RTP fields change.
  • COMPRESSED_RTP: the RTP header is compressed along with IP and UDP, used when the second-order difference is zero.
  • CONTEXT_STATE: sent from the decompressor back to the compressor to list contexts whose synchronization has or may have been lost.

With IPv6, a fifth type, COMPRESSED_NON_TCP from RFC 2507, MAY be used. Numeric codes for these packet types in PPP are to be assigned by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority.

In a COMPRESSED_RTP packet, a bit mask says which fields changed by other than the expected difference: I (IPv4 packet ID), U (UDP checksum), M (RTP marker bit), S (RTP sequence number), T (RTP timestamp) and L (CSRC count and list). The U bit is not sent: if the context has a nonzero UDP checksum, an unencoded 16-bit checksum is added to every later compressed packet until another uncompressed packet changes that. The L case is signaled by setting all of M, S, T and I (MSTI = 1111), which means an extended form with an extra byte and the CSRC list follows. If other fixed RTP fields change, such as payload type, the uncompressed RTP header MUST be sent.

Every compressed or full packet MUST carry the context ID and a 4-bit sequence number. Each context has its own sequence number space, so one lost packet invalidates only one context.
sections.eli5: There are a few kinds of notes. One is the whole label, used to start. Others say 'same as before, with these small changes'. And one goes backward to say 'I got confused, please start over'.

sections.title: Encoding the Differences
sections.content:
Changed values are sent as deltas using a variable-length encoding, so the common small values take few bytes. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to use a table-driven encoder and decoder, so that a table specific to a session can be negotiated, possibly even an optimal Huffman encoding.

The default encoding is built to handle the small changes seen in the IP ID and RTP sequence number when packets are lost upstream, while still fitting most audio and video deltas in two bytes. A value of 0 through 127 is sent directly in one byte. If the top two bits of the first byte are 10 or 11, the value continues into two or three bytes, using the low six bits of the first byte plus the next one or two bytes to form a 14- or 22-bit value. Negative deltas, which can come from misordered packets or the intentionally out-of-order timestamps on MPEG video, use otherwise redundant parts of the table, so a smaller range is covered.

An RTP timestamp change below -16384 or above 4194303 forces the RTP header to be sent uncompressed. Negative deltas for the 16-bit IP ID and RTP sequence number fields SHOULD be masked to 16 bits and encoded as large positive numbers.
sections.eli5: Small numbers get short names and big numbers get longer ones, like calling 'one' by a single letter but spelling out a huge number. Most changes are small, so most notes are very short.

sections.title: Detecting and Recovering from Loss
sections.content:
If the 4-bit sequence number for a context jumps by anything other than 1 (except when set by a FULL_HEADER or COMPRESSED_NON_TCP packet), the decompressor MUST invalidate that context and send a CONTEXT_STATE packet back. All packets for that context MUST be discarded until a full refresh arrives. The decompressor SHOULD limit how often it resends the message so it does not flood the reverse channel.

If the link layer reports an error, the decompressor MAY send an advisory CONTEXT_STATE listing the last valid sequence number and generation number for recently active contexts. The compressor may then mark a context invalid so its next packet is a full one. When the round-trip time is large compared with the packet spacing, several packets may be in flight, so some contexts can be invalidated unnecessarily.

Retransmission of a CONTEXT_STATE block is allowed, normally triggered by another packet arriving, or by a timer on the order of 1 second on a near-idle line. When UDP checksums are sent, the decompressor MAY try the twice algorithm from RFC 2507, applying the delta more than once and treating a checksum match as success, though there is a nontrivial risk of a false positive.

Some errors go unnoticed, for example if 16 packets are lost in a row and the link gives no error indication. So the decompressor is RECOMMENDED to verify the UDP checksum periodically, perhaps one packet in 16.
sections.eli5: Each note has a small counting number. If the receiver sees a number skip, it knows it missed something, so it tells the sender 'please send the whole label again' and ignores messages until then.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encryption removes the redundancy that this compression relies on, which gives some inducement to skip encryption on a slow link. Where encrypting data but not headers is acceptable, RTP offers an alternative method that encrypts only the payload, so compression can still be applied.

A faulty or malicious compressor could make the decompressor rebuild packets that do not match the originals but still have valid IP, UDP and RTP headers, possibly even valid UDP checksums. End-to-end authentication and integrity mechanisms are not affected by the compression and can detect this.

The CONTEXT_STATE packet is not authenticated. An attacker with access to the link could inject false ones and reduce compression efficiency, probably causing congestion, though such an attacker could disrupt the traffic in many other ways. The RFC also notes a denial-of-service risk for schemes with uneven decompression cost, and says this scheme does not show significant non-uniformity.
sections.eli5: Scrambling a message hides the patterns that make shrinking possible. Also, the 'start over' note has no password, so someone with access to the wire could fake it, but they could cause trouble in other ways anyway.

fields.name: Context ID (lsb)
fields.desc: Least significant bits of the session context ID; a most significant byte comes first if 16-bit CIDs are used.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Set when the RTP sequence number changed by other than the expected amount; a delta follows.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Set when the RTP timestamp changed by other than the expected amount; a delta follows.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Set when the IPv4 packet ID changed by other than the expected amount; a delta follows.

fields.name: Link sequence
fields.desc: 4-bit sequence number used to detect packet loss between compressor and decompressor.
